{"emails": [{"email_id": "email_email_7168baed8438", "folder": "INBOX", "sender": "pam.kowalski@northwindtech.com", "recipients": ["david.chen@moveops.com"], "subject": "Formal escalation: NorthWind account stability and retention decision", "content": "Hi David,

I am writing to you directly because we have not received the service recovery follow-through Catalina committed to on April 14, and at this point I do not think routing this back through her is appropriate.

NorthWind is now evaluating whether MoveOps can continue to support this account.

Two recent incidents have materially damaged confidence on our side:

First, Raj Patel's server lab relocation was handled in breach of the chain-of-custody requirements we stated in advance. The equipment was loaded before the required IT escort arrived and, as we understand it, was then placed into overnight warehouse storage despite explicit instructions that no interim storage was permitted.

Second, Emilia Cruz's piano was damaged during extraction. What has been equally concerning is the lack of timely, proactive communication afterward. Emilia should not have had to chase for accountability.

These are not isolated inconveniences. Combined with slow follow-up and missed commitments from your team, they have become a broader account confidence problem.

To be transparent, we have started preliminary conversations with PathFinder Logistics regarding Denver-area relocation support and broader account coverage. No decision has been made yet, but we are doing that diligence now.

If MoveOps wants to retain NorthWind's business, I need a concrete proposal from you by end of day Friday. That proposal should include:

1. A clear corrective action plan for the Raj Patel security incident, including ownership and documentation controls
2. A resolution path and reimbursement handling for Emilia Cruz's damage claim
3. Named account coverage going forward, with response-time expectations
4. Any commercial consideration you believe is appropriate given the service failures to date

Please treat this as a formal escalation and final warning before we decide whether to move this work elsewhere.

Pam Kowalski
Director of People Operations

The timing for this project is perfect — the expense review process is currently the most time-consuming aspect of our workflow. Here’s all the information you’ll need.

Standard Expense Categories

These are the categories we apply to all clients (though some clients may not cover all of them):

1. Equipment — laptops, monitors, keyboards, mice, webcams, docking stations, cables/adapters
2. Furniture — desks, non-ergonomic chairs, bookshelves, filing cabinets
3. Ergonomic — ergonomic chairs, standing desks, monitor arms, keyboard trays, wrist rests, footrests. This category is separate from general furniture because many clients have higher limits for ergonomic items.
4. Internet — setup fees for home internet, monthly service, mesh wifi systems, ethernet cables
5. Coworking — memberships for coworking spaces, day passes, meeting room rentals
6. Office Supplies — stationery, printer ink, paper, whiteboards, desk organizers
7. Travel — flights for team offsites or client visits (NOT for relocation, which is handled differently)

Common Edge Cases

These are the situations that often cause confusion:

- Bundled items: If someone purchases a 'keyboard + mouse combo' for $120, should it count as one equipment expense or two? We currently categorize it as one.
- Overlap between Ergonomic and Furniture: A standing desk could fit into either category. We place items marketed as 'ergonomic' or 'adjustable height' into the ergonomic category, which typically has a higher limit.
- Coworking memberships: These are usually recurring monthly. Some clients cover them, while others do not. The complexity arises when a client covers day passes but not monthly memberships.
- Internet setup versus monthly service: The first month of internet service often includes an installation fee ($100-200) along with the first month’s service. Some clients only reimburse for monthly service, excluding setup.
- Ergonomic items exceeding $500: Several clients set a cap for ergonomic items at $500 or $600. Employees frequently submit claims for ergonomic chairs priced between $450-550, which often leads to disputes.
- Monitor + arm combinations: A $400 monitor is categorized as equipment, while a $150 monitor arm is considered ergonomic. When these are purchased together as a bundle, categorization can become complicated.

Pilot Client Policies — Vectral Systems vs. Mosaic Robotics

These two clients are excellent candidates for piloting due to their significantly different policies:

Vectral Systems
- Equipment: up to $500 per item, receipts required
- Furniture: up to $400 per item, receipts required
- Ergonomic: up to $600 per item, receipts required (they increased this limit last quarter based on employee feedback)
- Internet: up to $150/month, receipts needed for setup only
- Coworking: NOT COVERED — explicitly excluded in their contract
- Office Supplies: up to $75 per item, no receipt required for items under $25
- Travel: handled separately, not included
- Contact: Rachel Whitfield (HR), collaborates with Mina from our side

Mosaic Robotics
- Equipment: up to $1,000 per item, receipts required for amounts over $200
- Furniture: up to $800 per item, receipts required
- Ergonomic: up to $800 per item (same limit as furniture — they do not differentiate)
- Internet: up to $200/month, receipts necessary
- Coworking: NOT COVERED — they maintain their own satellite offices and do not reimburse for coworking
- Office Supplies: up to $100 per item, no receipt required for items under $50
- Travel: handled separately
- Contact: Priya Delgado (Operations), works with Emeka from our side

⚠️ Important note on Mosaic: six months ago, they revised their coworking policy. They previously covered coworking up to $400/month but discontinued this when they opened satellite offices. Ensure the system reflects the current policy, not the outdated one. I’ve noticed operations team members mistakenly approving coworking expenses for Mosaic based on old information.

General Recommendations

- The option to 'flag for review' is crucial — when uncertain, DO NOT auto-deny. A wrongful rejection is more problematic than a delayed approval from the client's perspective. Employees become frustrated when legitimate expenses are denied.
- We need the capability for quick overrides. Currently, if an expense is incorrectly denied, it takes 1-2 days to resolve because it’s handled via email.
- Policy configurations should be easy to update. Clients tend to change their policies approximately once or twice a year, and we must be able to reflect those changes quickly.

I’ve attached the complete policy spreadsheet with all current clients (not just the two pilot cases). Let me know if you need anything else — I’m happy to discuss edge cases over a call.

Best,

{"emails": [{"email_id": "email_email_7168baed8438", "folder": "INBOX", "sender": "pam.kowalski@northwindtech.com", "recipients": ["david.chen@moveops.com"], "subject": "Formal escalation: NorthWind account stability and retention decision", "content": "Hi David,

I am writing to you directly because we have not received the service recovery follow-through Catalina committed to on April 14, and at this point I do not think routing this back through her is appropriate.

NorthWind is now evaluating whether MoveOps can continue to support this account.

Two recent incidents have materially damaged confidence on our side:

First, Raj Patel's server lab relocation was handled in breach of the chain-of-custody requirements we stated in advance. The equipment was loaded before the required IT escort arrived and, as we understand it, was then placed into overnight warehouse storage despite explicit instructions that no interim storage was permitted.

Second, Emilia Cruz's piano was damaged during extraction. What has been equally concerning is the lack of timely, proactive communication afterward. Emilia should not have had to chase for accountability.

These are not isolated inconveniences. Combined with slow follow-up and missed commitments from your team, they have become a broader account confidence problem.

To be transparent, we have started preliminary conversations with PathFinder Logistics regarding Denver-area relocation support and broader account coverage. No decision has been made yet, but we are doing that diligence now.

If MoveOps wants to retain NorthWind's business, I need a concrete proposal from you by end of day Friday. That proposal should include:

1. A clear corrective action plan for the Raj Patel security incident, including ownership and documentation controls
2. A resolution path and reimbursement handling for Emilia Cruz's damage claim
3. Named account coverage going forward, with response-time expectations
4. Any commercial consideration you believe is appropriate given the service failures to date

Please treat this as a formal escalation and final warning before we decide whether to move this work elsewhere.

Pam Kowalski
Director of People Operations

2. The joint calibration on the same unit is misaligned. Prototype Unit #2 and the control unit appear undamaged at this time, though we are scheduling a full diagnostic for both within the next 48 hours.

For context, each prototype is valued at $90,000. The total insured value for the pair is $180,000, as documented in the original relocation request I sent you on April 9. Blessing Okafor
Relocation Coordinator | MoveOps

input.content:
David, Catalina,

Per Chloe's ask, here is the operational read on the Emilia Cruz damage docket so the ops position is locked before the NorthWind package goes out. I've structured it the way we ran the Mosaic file last quarter: carrier exposure, client-facing disposition, and a process-improvement note on the file.

1) CARRIER EXPOSURE — closed on our side.
- KeyMove Specialty Transport (Craig Nguyen) documented the Steinway Model B scratch from the April 11 move: ~4.5–5" surface scratch on the bass-side rim near the keyboard cheek block, finish disruption, no structural crack. Crew Luis Romero / Ben Hall; contact reported ~11:07 AM at the second-floor landing.
- KeyMove added a $1,200 insurance rider to their bill. Marcus reviewed it on the finance side — the vendor paperwork lines up with the field report and there's no clean basis to dispute the vendor line, so it's being processed as submitted. That closes this ledger line.
- I've authorized Craig to open KeyMove's formal carrier claim now rather than hold it, so the damage resolution keeps moving. This is purely the carrier line and does not bind the client-facing decision below.

2) CLIENT-FACING DISPOSITION — open, your lane.
- Separate from the carrier claim, NorthWind/Emilia still need a disposition on how MoveOps makes this right (repair coverage, credit, or reimbursement). Pam's April 24 escalation names Emilia's damage claim as item #2 in the retention proposal, so this should be decided as part of the NorthWind package, not in isolation.
- Comms gap to own in that response: Emilia had to chase for accountability — Julian logged her same-day callback request on the 12th and it sat without an owner. Pam called the follow-up lag out specifically, so whatever the dollar treatment, the response should acknowledge it.
- I don't have authority on the commercial piece. What you'd need from ops to package it is in this note — the carrier facts above, confirmation the rider is handled, and the lesson below. I can supply the work order/intake docs for the file on request.

3) PROCESS IMPROVEMENT — captured on the file.
- Root operational cause: the walkup access assessment underestimated the turn radius out of the second-floor landing. I green-lit the extraction plan off a thin walkup assessment instead of requiring a pre-move site survey for a specialty/high-value instrument. The scratch was preventable with a survey.
- Corrective action I'm putting in place: a mandatory pre-move site survey before extraction on any specialty/high-value instrument move (pianos especially), so access geometry is verified before the instrument is touched.

Still moving on your side: the reimbursement/commercial treatment for Emilia and how it folds into the NorthWind retention proposal (Linear #482). I've left the operational facts on that Linear item for whoever picks up the file, and the relocation record is updated to reflect both the carrier and client-facing sides.

Blessing

input.text:
Capturing the operational lesson on the Emilia Cruz Steinway for the record:

Root cause of the scratch was an access-assessment gap, not crew handling. The walkup turn radius out of the second-floor landing was tighter than our access assessment indicated, and the piano had to be over-rotated to clear the railing/wall corner — that's where the bass-side rim made contact. I green-lit the extraction off a thin walkup assessment when a specialty instrument like a Steinway warranted a pre-move site survey first. That's on me, and the scratch was preventable.

Corrective action going forward: *mandatory pre-move site survey before extraction on any specialty/high-value instrument move (pianos especially)* — verify access geometry before anyone touches the instrument; don't treat it as a tough stair carry.

KeyMove has the carrier claim (rider processed as submitted, finance reviewed). The client-facing reimbursement piece is with David/Catalina as part of the NorthWind retention package. Flagging this so it lands in our playbook and doesn't repeat. cc <@moveops_chloe_vance>
